feedback: If the pupil appends a zero (3.5 km → '3.50 m') or uses the wrong factor (3.5 km → '350 m', i.e. ×100), show the digits' positions on the chart: ×1000 moves each digit three places left past a fixed point, so 3.5 lands as 3500.
If direction is reversed (3.5 km → 0.0035 m), re-ask 'metres are smaller, so are there more or fewer than 3.5?' — more, so multiply, so the answer is bigger than 3.5.
Add a reasonableness check every time: 'Is your answer bigger or smaller than you started with, and does that fit the unit size?'
activities.intendedInsight: The number grows (or shrinks) because the DIGITS move a fixed number of places, not because zeros are 'added' — so 3.5 km can never become 3.50 m.
learnerActions: Enter a measurement such as 3.5 km and choose the target unit (metres).
Before computing, answer the prompt: 'Is a metre bigger or smaller than a kilometre — so will there be MORE metres or FEWER?' State whether this means multiply or divide.

Watch (or physically move, using a place-value chart or Gattegno chart) every digit slide three places left while the decimal point stays nailed in place, so 3.5 becomes 3500, with place-holder zeros dropping in where needed.
Repeat for a case that keeps the decimal visible, e.g. 1.75 km to m, naming where each digit lands (the 1 becomes 1 thousand, giving 1750 m).
Do at least one divide case too, e.g. 4500 m to km, moving digits three places right to give 4.5 km.
activities.title: Slide the digits across a fixed decimal point

feedback: If a pupil pattern-copies without the ×10 idea, ask what single multiplication turns the left column into the right (auto-checking each row against ×10 makes a broken row visible immediately).
Correct answers for the cm→mm table: 1→10, 2→20, 5→50, 10→100.
activities.intendedInsight: A conversion table is a repeated multiplication by the same factor, not a copied number pattern — understanding the factor lets you extend or correct any row.
learnerActions: Complete a cm→mm table: 1→__, 2→__, 5→__, 10→__ and say what you multiply by for each row.
Read the completed table aloud as a set of equivalent multiplications ('each centimetre is ten millimetres — I'm multiplying by 10').
Check each row against the ×10 relationship and flag any row that breaks the pattern, explaining why it is wrong.
Build a second table for a different pair of units (e.g. kg→g, ×1000) to see the same structure with a different multiplier.
activities.title: Build and check conversion tables

feedback: If justification is only 'that's the rule', redirect to unit size: which unit is bigger, so are there more or fewer of the target unit?
For the true/false item: 25.34 × 10 = 253.4, NOT 25.340 — appending a zero does not multiply a decimal by 10; the digits move one place left.
activities.intendedInsight: The operation follows from which unit is bigger and how many of the smaller unit fit in it — the heuristic 'fewer of the bigger unit → divide' decides direction every time.
learnerActions: For a mix of conversions (some to smaller units, some to larger), first state 'multiply' or 'divide' and why, using unit size, BEFORE working the answer.
Answer true/false checks that target the zero error, e.g. 'Is 25.34 × 10 = 25.340?' and explain.
For each worked conversion, say aloud 'did I multiply or divide, and how did I know?'
activities.title: Choose and justify the operation before calculating
